sentences.text: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a raven, featuring broad, rounded wings and a long tail relative to its body.
The Munich Specimen is missing only the front of its face.
The Thermopolis Specimen has the best-preserved head and feet, but most of the neck and lower jaw are not preserved.
The Schamhaupten Specimen is the only known specimen lacking preserved feathers.
Archaeopteryx was first named based on a single feather discovered in 1861.
The initial Archaeopteryx specimen was the first dinosaur found to possess feathers.
Twelve additional fossils of Archaeopteryx have been discovered since the initial announcement.
All known Archaeopteryx fossils originate from limestone deposits near Solnhofen, Germany.
The Unnumbered Specimen was originally classified as Compsognathus by the amateur collector Friedrich Müller.
Studies of the eleventh specimen revealed previously unknown plumage features, including feathers on the upper and lower legs and metatarsus, as well as the only preserved tail tip.
Despite having broad wings and an inferred ability to fly or glide, Archaeopteryx shared more features with small Mesozoic dinosaurs than with modern birds.
The presence of feathers in Archaeopteryx suggests it may have been warm-blooded.
The Thermopolis Specimen shows that Archaeopteryx lacked a reversed toe, implying a terrestrial or trunk-climbing lifestyle rather than the ability to perch on branches.
Archaeopteryx was named by Meyer in 1861 and is a conserved name.
The type species of Archaeopteryx is Archaeopteryx lithographica.
Two other species have been described: A. siemensii by Dames in 1897 and A. albersdoerferi by Kundrat et al. in 2018.
Archaeopteryx lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago.
Most Archaeopteryx specimens were found in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany, dating to the early Tithonian stage of the Jurassic period (150.8–148.5 million years ago).
The Schamhaupten Specimen is from the Painten Formation and is somewhat older than other specimens.
Archaeopteryx fossils date to the Late Jurassic period.
It is debated whether all discovered remains of Archaeopteryx belong to a single species or at least a single genus.
Further analyses suggest the Haarlem Specimen differs little from certified Archaeopteryx except for a markedly larger size.
Analyses suggested the Mühlheim Specimen belongs to a more advanced avialan lineage close to Jeholornis and the ancestors of Sapeornis.
In 1985, a group led by Fred Hoyle and Lee Spetner claimed that the feathers on the Berlin and London Archaeopteryx specimens were forged.
